sources.title: VESA — Why DisplayPort
quotes: Up to 5.4 Gbps per lane–21.6 Gbps over 4 lanes
Up to 8.1 Gbps per lane–32.4 Gbps over 4 lanes
Allowing for overhead — 25.92 Gbps over 4 lanes
Maximum link rate to up to 20 Gbps/lane and features more efficient 128b/132b channel coding, delivering a maximum payload of 77.37 Gbps

sources.title: VESA — early certification program for HBR3
quotes: DisplayPort’s new HBR3 data rate supports a total bandwidth of 32.4 Gbps when using all four lanes in the DisplayPort or USB Type-C connector, at 8.1 Gbps per lane. This provides a combined audio/video payload data rate of 25.92 Gbps
By using the DisplayPort Multi-Stream feature, this bandwidth can also be shared among multiple monitors connected to a dock.

sources.title: VESA / AMD — Display Summit USA 2016 (DisplayPort link-rate table)
quotes: Main Link Configuration | Raw Bit Rate (includes coding overhead) - Gbps | Application Bandwidth Throughput - Gbps
Flexible lane configuration allows 1, 2, or 4 lanes to be enabled

sources.title: VESA — UHBR device certification and DP40/DP80 cables
quotes: VESA certified DP40 cables must support up to the UHBR10 link rate

VESA certified DP80 cables must support up to the UHBR20 link rate (20 Gbps) defined by DisplayPort 2.0, with four lanes, providing a maximum throughput of 80 Gbps. VESA certified DP80 cables will also support the UHBR13.5 link rate (13.5 Gbps)

sources.title: VESA — DisplayPort on the USB Type-C connector (DP Alt Mode)
quotes: The DisplayPort Alt Mode repurposes some or all of the four existing SuperSpeed USB lanes to deliver full DisplayPort performance

sources.title: VESA — DisplayPort Alt Mode overview
quotes: A passive Full Feature USB Type-C to Type-C cable can carry up to four DisplayPort lanes
Implemented with two high speed pairs for DP (using two lane DP operation), and two high speed pairs for USB
USB 2.0 or 3.1 Data

sources.title: HDMI Forum — HDMI Specification 2.0 release
quotes: offers a significant increase in bandwidth (up to 18Gbps) to support new features such as 4K@50/60 (2160p)

sources.title: HDMI Licensing Administrator — HDMI 2.1
quotes: The Ultra High Speed HDMI Cable was introduced in the HDMI 2.1 Specification and entered the market in 2020. It is applicable for system configurations supporting up to 48Gbps maximum bandwidth.

sources.title: Microsoft Support — Troubleshoot external monitor connections in Windows
quotes: press the Windows logo key + P to make sure that the Extend option is selected
Disconnect all accessories from your PC. Connected docks, dongles, adapters and other hardware can cause conflicts.
Try changing the cable connecting the external monitor. If the new one works, you know the previous cable was faulty.
If your system has more than one video output port, try plugging your external monitor into one of the other video output ports.
pressing Windows logo Key + Ctrl + Shift + B to reset your graphics driver may fix your issue. If this does not work, see if restarting helps.

If you are trying to use a display splitter to extend your display to more than one external monitor, you won't be able to. The splitter is duplicating the same signal instead of creating two independent signals.

sources.title: Microsoft Support — Fix USB-C problems in Windows
quotes: Display connection might be limited
Make sure your PC, the external display, and the cable all support DisplayPort or MHL alternate modes. Make sure the device or dongle is connected directly to your PC.
The device or dongle is connected to your PC using an external hub or dock. There are too many other devices or dongles connected to your PC that use a USB-C connection.

sources.title: Microsoft Support — Change the refresh rate on your monitor in Windows
quotes: Select Start > Settings > System > Display > Advanced display
The Display information panel shows the current resolution and refresh rate for the selected display, and whether the display supports variable refresh rate (VRR).
The refresh rates that appear depend on your display and what it supports.
The refresh rate dropdown list shows an asterisk (*) next to refresh rates that don't support your current resolution.

sources.title: Microsoft Learn — Windows USB Type-C troubleshooting notifications
quotes: Display connection might be limited Make sure the DisplayPort device you're connecting to is supported by your PC.
DisplayPort Alternate Mode SVID 0xFF01 (or the MHL Alternate Mode SVID 0xFF02) is present in the wSVID field.

sources.title: Microsoft Support — Connect Surface to an external display
quotes: Make sure that your external display is turned on and its input source set to the port you are connecting to.
Use the shortest possible cable to connect your Surface to your monitor, as overly long cables can lead to connectivity problems

sources.title: Plugable KB — Can I connect my high refresh rate monitor to a Plugable dock?
quotes: Most Plugable docks do not officially support monitors over 60Hz including 120Hz or 144Hz refresh rate unless otherwise specified on the Plugable product page or listing.

DisplayLink USB Graphics technology and Silicon Motion based docking stations and graphics adapters, like our USB 3.0 dual display and USB Type-C triple display docking stations, are limited to 60Hz refresh rate by the USB graphics controller hardware.

USB Type-C DisplayPort Alternate Mode docking station and ports on our USB Type-C Triple Display Docking Stations can support higher refresh rates, but may be limited by the computer's capability and available bandwidth to the docking station.

sources.title: Plugable KB — How to determine your USB-C port video capabilities
quotes: DisplayPort video data is transmitted directly from the USB-C port, taking up two or four of the USB SuperSpeed data lines.
DisplayPort 1.2 capable hosts can support a single 4K 60Hz display and USB 2.0 data, or single 4K 30Hz display and USB 10Gbps data (for example when using a docking station).
DisplayPort 1.4 capable hosts can support a single 8K 30Hz/4K 120Hz display and USB 2.0 data, or a single 4K 60Hz display and USB 10Gbps data.
Thunderbolt 4 & USB4 enables two DisplayPort 1.4 streams, supporting a single 8K display, or upto two 4K 60Hz displays
Not all USB-C ports support video output. Checking your laptop's documentation is crucial to confirm this capability.

sources.title: Plugable KB — "Display connection might be limited" with a USB-C dock or adapter
quotes: The USB-C port on the laptop itself does not support video out of its USB-C port. In other words, the USB-C port on the laptop supports data transfer only.
The USB-C cable being used to connect the USB-C device to the laptop is not a compatible cable, and may support data transfer/charging only (no video support).

There is a some kind of USB-C adapter in between the laptop and and USB-C device, and this adapter does not support USB-C video. Please remove the adapter and try connecting the device directly to the system.

sources.title: Plugable KB — How to set the display refresh rate in Windows 11
quotes: If the desired refresh rate is not available, confirm that the display, computer or graphics hardware, docking station or adapter, and video cable all support the desired resolution and refresh rate combination.
Some devices may support a higher refresh rate only at a lower display resolution.

quotes: DSC compression ratios are not set in stone, some computers enable 2.4:1
The operating system is not made aware of any of these settings, it won't report the DisplayPort Version (1.2, 1.4, 2.0 etc), nor will it report if DSC is available, or the DSC compression ratio.
